correctness.rationale: Lucas's theorem applied to the digits of m=2n shows that nonzero binomial(4n,2n) modulo 5 occurs precisely when every base-five digit of m is at most two. Its residue is i^h in {+1,-1}, where h is the even number of one-digits. Explicit carry matrices A_d have sum [[2,i],[i,2]] and the nonzero-state indicator matrices sum [[2,1],[1,2]]; their eigenvalues give respectively Re((1+i)(2+i)^L) and 3^L. Fixed high-digit products have operator norm at most sqrt(2); aligned base-five interval partitions and the spectral norm sqrt(5)^j give O(sqrt(X)). The nonintegral rational number 6/5 prevents ((2+i)/sqrt(5))^2 from being a root of unity and gives a dense phase orbit, proving limsup normalized absolute imbalance sqrt(2). The bundled verifier independently checks 200 literal binomial coefficients, 78125 Lucas products, seven block counts, and all initial partial sums in that range. The proof supplies all universal quantifiers; finite checks alone do not.

originality.rationale: Theorem 4.1 of arXiv:1701.06217 gives the prior 0/1/4 residue support, crediting Vsemirnov; it does not count the two nonzero classes or give discrepancy. arXiv:1301.7651 provides the older binomial-residue problem but no such distribution. Berend-Harmse 1998 treats all central binomial indices rather than the exceptional even subsequence, whose nonzero residues cannot be uniform across all four units. The full Barat-Grabner 2001 manuscript gives general digit-block asymptotics for Pascal-triangle distributions but no statement of this diagonal two-residue exact identity, global sharp square-root error, or limit-point interval. Three targeted repository searches returned no matching equivalent; their unrelated nearest hits cannot prove uniqueness. Residual risk from unlocated direct specializations remains. The claim is the new exact quantitative statement, not the classical automaton method or support restriction.

value.rationale: The exceptional central binomial subsequence is already a published counterexample to a natural binomial-residue conjecture: residues 2 and 3 vanish identically, making the balance of the remaining two nonzero classes a specific natural invariant. The theorem determines both class sizes exactly for every digital length, controls signed imbalance at all cutoffs with square-root error, and proves the optimal exponent and complete normalized limit-point interval. This is a sharp quantitative distribution law on a sparse fractal support of cardinality 3^L, not an arbitrary small case, a restatement of Lucas's theorem, or a numerical census.
